Mini-CLIP on Flickr8k · a visual breakdown

How a photo and a sentence end up in the same place

We trained a small CLIP: a ResNet-18 reads the photo, a two-block Transformer reads the caption, and a contrastive loss pulls the two into one 256-number space. This page follows one photo and its caption through every step. Pick a photo below; every interactive figure follows it.

These four are real test photos from the run, with their first human caption. Each one is also a point in the before/after embedding maps in section 7, so you can find it there.

This post covers
  1. What CLIP is, the problem it solves, and the two-encoder plan
  2. The image encoder, layer by layer, on your chosen photo
  3. The text encoder on the same photo's caption, including attention
  4. The similarity matrix and the loss: Li2t, Lt2i and their average
  5. Backpropagation and the weight update
  6. Training, live: a toy you can run, then the real 20-epoch run
  7. The shared space before and after training, in 2D and 3D
  8. Results, conclusion and references

Every figure carries a tag. Actual Run means the numbers or plot come from the trained Flickr8k model. live on this photo means the browser is computing it right now on the photo you picked. toy weights means the mechanism is exact but the weights are random or small, because the trained weights aren't in this page.

1The concept and the problem

CLIP (Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training, Radford et al., 2021) learns to put a photo and a sentence that describes it at the same point in a shared space. Once that works you can search photos with a sentence, caption a photo by finding the nearest sentence, or classify a photo with no classifier at all, just by writing the class names as sentences.

The problem. A photo is a 224×224×3 block of pixel intensities. A caption is a list of words. Nothing about the two is directly comparable: there is no sensible way to subtract "dog" from a brown pixel. And Flickr8k has no labels like "dog" or "beach". All we have is 8,091 photos, each with five sentences people wrote about it.

The idea. Use the caption itself as the label. Build two separate networks that each end in the same kind of output, a list of 256 numbers scaled to length 1:

The whole pipeline on one page

Architecture

Top lane: the image encoder. Bottom lane: the text encoder. They share nothing except the size of their output. The only place they meet is the similarity matrix, and the only signal that trains them is the loss computed from it (dashed arrows = gradients flowing back).

Training takes a batch of N photo–caption pairs (N = 128 in the run; N = 4 in the examples on this page). Both encoders run, giving N image vectors v and N text vectors t. Every image is compared with every caption, which gives an N×N grid of cosine similarities. The N true pairs sit on the diagonal. The loss rewards the diagonal for being large and everything else for being small. It is contrastive: each true pair is learned against 127 wrong ones in the same batch.

A few data details from the notebook that matter later. The split is by photo, never by caption, so no test photo was ever seen in training. Each epoch pairs every photo with one random caption out of its five. Photos get a random crop and colour jitter but no horizontal flip, because flipping would turn "left" into "right" and make the caption wrong.

2The image encoder, step by step

The image encoder is a ResNet-18, written by hand in the notebook with torchvision's layer names so the ImageNet weights load into it. The classification head is removed. What's left turns a photo into 512 numbers, and one Linear layer turns those into the 256-number vector v. Here is every stage, on your photo.

2.1From a photo to numbers

The photo is resized and centre-cropped to 224×224. Each pixel is three numbers between 0 and 255: red, green, blue. Hover over the photo to read the pixels under the cursor.

Pixels under the cursor

live on this photo
224 × 224 input (hover / drag)
6×6 patch, zoomed: R G B per pixel

2.2Three channels, then normalise

The network doesn't see one picture. It sees three stacked grids, one per colour, a tensor of shape 3×224×224. Each value is divided by 255 and then standardised with the ImageNet mean and standard deviation, because that's what the pretrained weights expect:

x̂c = (xc/255 − μc) / σc    μ = (0.485, 0.456, 0.406), σ = (0.229, 0.224, 0.225)

The 3×224×224 tensor

live on this photo

Bright = high value after normalisation. Values now sit roughly between −2 and +2.6, centred near 0, which keeps the first layer's outputs in a healthy range.

2.3The first convolution: 64 filters slide over the photo

conv1 has 64 filters, each 7×7×3. A filter is a small stencil. At each position it multiplies its 147 weights with the 147 pixel values under it and adds them up into one number. It then moves 2 pixels (stride 2), so the 224×224 input becomes a 112×112 output, one output map per filter: 64×112×112.

The filters below are the actual first-layer filters from Actual Run, read back from the notebook's filter plot. Some respond to edges at an angle, some to a colour blob. Pick one and watch it sweep over your photo.

conv1: 7×7×3 filter, stride 2

live on this photo
Actual Run's 64 conv1 filters (click one)
hover the output map to inspect any position
input 224×224 · window 7×7
output map 112×112 for this filter

patch
filter

Filter weights are Actual Run's real conv1 filters, recovered from the plotted image, so their overall scale is approximate but their pattern is right. The arithmetic is the real convolution, computed in your browser.

2.4BatchNorm and ReLU

Each of the 64 maps is then normalised by BatchNorm (shift and scale so it has a stable mean and spread) and passed through ReLU, which keeps positive values and sets every negative value to 0. ReLU is what makes the network non-linear. Without it, all the stacked layers would collapse into one big linear map.

16 of the 64 maps after conv1 → BN → ReLU

live on this photo
values of the selected map: before vs after ReLU

Same photo, 16 different detectors. Click a map to select its filter. Bright means "this pattern is here".

2.5Max-pooling: keep the strongest response

A 3×3 max-pool with stride 2 slides over each map and keeps only the largest value in each window. 112×112 becomes 56×56. The map gets four times smaller, and small shifts in the photo stop mattering much, since the maximum survives a one-pixel nudge.

MaxPool 3×3, stride 2

live on this photo
a 7×7 corner of the ReLU map (values)
→ 3×3 pooled
whole map: 112×112 → 56×56

2.6Four residual stages: bigger patterns, smaller maps

Now come four stages, layer1 to layer4, each made of two BasicBlocks. A block applies conv3×3 → BN → ReLU → conv3×3 → BN, then adds its own input back before the last ReLU. That skip connection gives gradients a short path back to early layers, which is why a ResNet can be deep and still train.

One BasicBlock, and the shape of the tensor through the stages

your architecture

Each stage after the first halves the width and height (stride 2) and doubles the channels: 56×56×64 → 28×28×128 → 14×14×256 → 7×7×512. Each value in a deeper map is computed from a larger area of the photo, its receptive field. By layer4 one cell "sees" more than the whole image, so the 512 channels there describe things like "furry animal" or "sandy ground" rather than edges.

How much of the photo one cell sees

live on this photo

2.7Global average pooling: 7×7×512 → 512

The last map is 512 channels of 7×7. Global average pooling takes the mean of each 7×7 grid, one number per channel. The result is a 512-number summary of the whole photo, with no positions left in it.

Average each channel's 7×7 grid

toy values
one channel at layer4 (7×7)
the 512-number feature vector h

The 7×7 grid here is your photo's conv1 response averaged down to 7×7, standing in for a real layer4 channel. The 512 bars are illustrative. Shapes and arithmetic are exactly the model's.

2.8Project into the shared space and normalise

One Linear layer, proj: 512 → 256, maps h into the shared space. This layer is new and starts random; it's where the image side learns to "speak the same language" as the text side. Then the vector is divided by its own length, so every image ends on the surface of a 256-dimensional unit sphere:

u = Wimg h + b   (256 numbers)     v = u / ‖u‖   so ‖v‖ = 1

h (512) → u (256) → v = u/‖u‖

toy weights

That's the image encoder end to end: photo → 3×224×224 → conv1 64×112×112 → pool 64×56×56 → layer1–4 → 512×7×7 → GAP 512 → Linear 256 → normalise → v. After training, we can ask which pixels pushed v toward its caption. Grad-CAM answers that by sending the gradient of cos(v, t) back to layer4:

What the trained image encoder looks at for its own caption

Actual Run

3The text encoder, on the same photo's caption

The other half reads the caption. It's a small Transformer: token and position embeddings, two pre-LayerNorm blocks with 4 attention heads each, then the vector of a special [CLS] token becomes the caption vector t. Embedding size 256, like the shared space.

3.1Tokenise: words → ids

The caption is lower-cased and split into words with the regex [a-z0-9']+, so punctuation disappears and "wall-ride" becomes two words. A [CLS] token goes in front. Each word is looked up in a vocabulary built from the training captions (words seen fewer than 3 times become [UNK]).

Caption → tokens → ids

live on this caption
raw caption
tokens with ids

ids 0, 1, 2 are reserved for [PAD], [CLS], [UNK], and every other word is numbered by how common it is. The word ids shown are ranks among the 600 test captions in this page, a stand-in for the training vocabulary.

3.2Batch and pad

Captions have different lengths, but a batch must be a rectangle. Shorter captions are padded with [PAD] (id 0) up to the longest one in the batch, and a mask records which positions are padding so attention can ignore them. Here is our batch of four.

Token batch: 4 × L

live on this batch

Grey dashed cells are padding: pad_mask = (ids == 0). True means "attention, don't look here".

3.3Token embedding + position embedding

Each id selects a row from a learned table (nn.Embedding(vocab, 256)). Attention has no sense of order, so a second table adds a learned vector for each position 0, 1, 2… The input to the Transformer is the sum: x = tok[id] + pos[i], one 256-number row per token.

x = token embedding + position embedding

toy weights

One row per token, first 32 of the 256 dimensions shown. Blue negative, red positive. In the run these tables start as small random numbers (std 0.02 and 0.01) and are learned.

3.4Self-attention, one step at a time

Attention lets every token gather information from the other tokens. Each token makes a query ("what am I looking for?"), a key ("what do I contain?") and a value ("what do I pass on?"). A token's output is a weighted average of all values, weighted by how well its query matches each key. Step through it below, or press play.

One attention head inside block 1

toy weights
who does the selected token read? (click a token)

The formula for one head, with dk = 256/4 = 64 in the run:

Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax( QKᵀ/√dk + mask ) · V    Q = LN(x)WQ, K = LN(x)WK, V = LN(x)WV

Four heads run side by side, each with its own WQ, WK, WV, so each can look for a different relation. Their outputs are concatenated and mixed by WO.

3.5The rest of the block, twice

A block is x ← x + MHA(LN(x)), then x ← x + MLP(LN(x)), where the MLP is 256 → 1024 → GELU → 256. LayerNorm comes before each sub-layer ("pre-LN"), which makes small Transformers train more stably. The model stacks two blocks. After block 2, every token's row has mixed in information from the whole caption.

3.6Read [CLS], project, normalise

[CLS] carries no word of its own, so its final row is a pure summary of what it gathered through attention. That row goes through a final LayerNorm, a Linear 256 → 256, and is normalised to length 1. That's t.

[CLS] row → LN → Linear → t (‖t‖ = 1)

toy weights

4Combine: the similarity matrix and the loss

Now both encoders have run on the batch. We have four image vectors v1..4 and four caption vectors t1..4, all of length 1. Because they have length 1, their dot product is the cosine of the angle between them: 1 means same direction, 0 means unrelated.

sij = vi · tj     logitsij = sij / τ

τ is the temperature, a single learned number that starts at 0.07. Dividing by a small τ stretches the cosines apart before the softmax, so the model can be confident.

The loss looks at the matrix twice. Row-wise (image → text): for photo i, softmax over the four captions should put its probability on caption i. Column-wise (text → image): for caption j, softmax over the four photos should pick photo j. Each is a cross-entropy, the negative log of the probability given to the right answer:

Li2t = −(1/N) Σi log [ esii/τ / Σj esij/τ ] softmax along each row
Lt2i = −(1/N) Σj log [ esjj/τ / Σi esij/τ ] softmax down each column
L = ( Li2t + Lt2i ) / 2

Drag the slider from "before training" to "after training" and watch the numbers.

The batch of four, start to finish

computed live
① cosine similarity sij = vi·tj
② logits = s / τ
③ softmax along rows → p(caption j | photo i)
④ softmax down columns → p(photo i | caption j)

Diagonal cosines after training are Actual Run's real values for these four photos with their own captions (from the Grad-CAM figure). Off-diagonal values and the "before" matrix are illustrative. Before training they match the run's averages (matched ≈ mismatched ≈ 0.04). After training we made the two photos of people deliberately confusable with each other's captions, so the softmax has real work to do. τ before = 0.070, after = 0.037, both from Actual Run. Chance level for N = 4 is ln 4 = 1.386; for the run's N = 128 it's ln 128 = 4.85.

5Backpropagation: how the loss moves the weights

The loss is one number. Training asks: if I nudge each weight a little, does the loss go up or down? The chain rule answers that for all ~11 million image weights and all text weights in one backward pass, starting at the loss and walking back through every operation.

5.1The gradient at the similarity matrix

For softmax plus cross-entropy the first step is very clean. The gradient of L with respect to each logit is "what the model predicted minus what it should have predicted":

∂L/∂logitij = ½ · [ (Pij − 𝟙[i=j]) + (Qij − 𝟙[i=j]) ] / N P = row softmax, Q = column softmax

On the diagonal this is negative: "increase this similarity". Off the diagonal it's positive: "decrease this one", and more so the more probability the wrong pair stole. Gradient descent moves opposite the gradient.

∂L/∂logits for the current batch

computed live

Follows the slider in section 4. Green cells (negative gradient) will be pushed up, red cells pushed down. As training proceeds and P approaches the identity matrix, every entry shrinks toward 0 and learning slows. That's what convergence looks like.

5.2The pull and the push on each vector

One step further back, the gradient reaches the vectors themselves. For image vector vi:

−∂L/∂vi = (1/τ) [ (1 − Pii)·ti − Σj≠i Pij·tj ] (row part; the column part adds the same shape)

So vi is pulled toward its own caption and pushed away from every other caption, each push weighted by how confusable that caption currently is. Captions feel the mirror-image forces. Below is a 2D version you can step by hand: 4 photos and 4 captions as unit vectors on a circle.

Gradient forces on the circle

toy 2D vectors

Circles are photos, triangles are captions, colours mark which pair belongs together. Arrows show −∂L/∂v for the selected photo (click any circle): the green arrow pulls it toward its own caption, the red arrows push it away from the others. Their sum, the thick arrow, is the direction gradient descent moves it. After the move, the vector is renormalised back onto the circle.

5.3Back through both encoders

From v and t the gradient keeps going: through the length-1 normalisation (which removes the part of the gradient that would only change the length), through each projection layer, then down through the ResNet on one side and the Transformer on the other. Every weight receives its own ∂L/∂w. This is the one place the two encoders interact: the image weights are shaped by the captions, and the text weights by the photos.

Where the gradient goes

Architecture

5.4The weight update

With every gradient in hand, the optimiser takes one step. The run uses AdamW, which keeps a running average of each weight's gradient (m) and of its square (v), and steps by their ratio, so every weight moves at a sensible rate. Weight decay shrinks weights slightly each step.

m ← β₁m + (1−β₁)g    v ← β₂v + (1−β₂)g²    m̂ = m/(1−β₁ᵏ), v̂ = v/(1−β₂ᵏ)
w ← w − lr · ( m̂ / (√v̂ + ε) + λ·w )

Specifics from the notebook: lr = 3×10⁻⁴ for the new layers and the Transformer, 10× smaller (3×10⁻⁵) for the pretrained ResNet so its ImageNet knowledge isn't wiped out, weight decay λ = 0.05 (not on biases, norms or the temperature), and lr = 2×10⁻³ for the temperature because it's a single number that otherwise moves slowly. One epoch of warm-up, then cosine decay to 0. Gradients are clipped to norm 1, mixed precision is on, and τ is clamped at ≥ 0.01.

Forward pass, loss, backward pass, update: that's one step. One epoch is 46 steps (5,900 training photos ÷ 128), and the run does 20 epochs.

Here are 600 test photos and their captions in the shared space, before training and after, in the same projection style the notebook uses (PCA of photos and captions together, so they share axes). BEFORE training

Before training, photos and captions are two separate islands. The ResNet already produces meaningful features (it's ImageNet-pretrained), but the projection and the whole text encoder are random, so there's nothing linking the two sides. After training the islands overlap and, coloured by theme, the space is organised by meaning: dogs near dogs, snow near snow, and each photo's caption lands among similar photos.

9Conclusion

With nothing but photos and the sentences people wrote about them, the model learned a shared space where a caption lands near its photo. Two independent encoders, a ResNet-18 and a two-block Transformer, were trained only through an N×N similarity matrix and the symmetric loss (Li2t + Lt2i)/2. Test recall went from chance to R@10 = 65% (image → text) and 57% (text → image), and the space organises itself by themes the model was never told about, well enough for 59% zero-shot classification.

What the run also shows:

  • It overfits early. Validation loss flattens at about 2.4 from epoch 5 while training loss keeps falling to 0.6. With ~6,000 training photos the text encoder can memorise captions. More data, stronger augmentation or freezing more of the ResNet would help more than more epochs.
  • The modality gap shrinks but doesn't close. Gap 1.02 → 0.14 and kNN mixing 0 → 0.28. Retrieval works anyway, because only relative similarity matters.
  • The temperature matters. It fell from 0.070 to 0.037 on its own, sharpening the softmax as the model got more certain.
  • Scale is the gap to real CLIP. Same idea, but OpenAI trained on 400 million pairs with batch size 32,768. Each extra negative in the batch makes the task harder and the space better.
